It fails to compare against standard ensemble baselines (e.g., uniform averaging, simple softmax weighting, or Hedge). Given that the method essentially performs a form of adaptive weighting without training, there is no evidence presented that the complex stochastic filtering mechanism outperforms a trivial static average or a simpler online weighting heuristic. The claimed 17% F1 gain is likely an artifact of ensembling multiple models rather than the specific filtering dynamics. Without this comparison, the central premise of the paper remains unproven.
2.  **Insufficient Experimental Scope:** The claim that MoE-F is a "viable online mixture of expert framework" for "various other challenging tasks" is not supported by any evidence beyond a single, small financial dataset (NIFTY, 317 steps). As noted in the "Novel Insights" section, the performance gain is almost entirely driven by the majority class (Neutral). The method performs *worse* than the best individual expert on the critical minority class (Fall) and is not significantly better on the other class (Rise). The aggregate F1 metric masks the fact that the method fails to improve on the most difficult, imbalanced predictions. This suggests the method is an imbalance corrector rather than a robust prediction engine, yet the paper promotes it as a general improvement.
